newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi announces military service for students.
newsitem.headline: Burundi announces military service for students.

text.p: Burundi's main university said on Friday all first and second year students were being called up for one year of military service.
It was the latest step in a programme to bolster Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army since it took power in a coup last July.
Burundi's main Hutu-dominated Frodebu party, ousted from power by the coup, condemned the plan as "national suicide".
"It's national suicide because war is not the solution.... The only solution is a ceasefire and the immediate start of negotiations,"said Frodebu Secretary-General Augustin Nzojibwami.
Around 3,000 students will be required from the new academic year in September to undertake three months of training and nine months of duty, said university rector Gilbert Midende.

"The next academic year will be different as the government has instituted military service to apply to students who are in the first year and second year," Midende told Bujumbura-based Studio Ijambo radio.
Virtually all 5,000 students at university are members of the Tutsi minority and the main campuses in the capital and second town Gitega are known as hotbeds of Tutsi radicalism.

A human rights report said Tutsi students at Gitega helped security forces kill up to 30 Hutu fellow students shortly after the coup. Hutu students fled the Bujumbura campus after up to 50 were killed in June 1995.
Students closed down Bujumbura university shortly before the coup and frequently demonstrate against Hutus and Tutsi leaders.
Burundi's army was around 25,000-strong last July but its ranks swelled with the recruitment of thousands of Tutsi militiamen after the coup, a diplomat in Bujumbura said.
More than 150,000 people, the majority civilians, have died since October 1993 in massacres and Burundi's civil war, which pits the army against Hutu rebels.
Tutsi Pierre Buyoya took power in the coup claiming only he could save the country from sliding into genocide, but human rights groups say massacres by the army and rebels continue.
